```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
library(iscm)
```

This vignette walks through a complete iSCM analysis, in the order recommended
by Di Stefano and Mellace: estimate, check the diagnostics, choose the
specification, run the placebo analysis, and check the sensitivity to the set of
potentially affected units. The last section replicates the paper's application
to German reunification.

## The idea in one paragraph

Standard synthetic control methods (SCM) require the donor pool to contain only
units that are unaffected by the intervention. This is restrictive when some
donors are themselves treated, or exposed to spillovers, yet are essential for a
good pre-intervention fit. Because SCM weights are estimated on
**pre-intervention data only**, fitting a synthetic control for the main treated
unit and for each potentially affected unit yields a linear system

$$\hat\beta_t = \hat\Omega\,\vartheta_t - B_t,$$

where $\hat\beta_t$ collects the contaminated gaps, $\hat\Omega$ has ones on the
diagonal and minus the estimated cross-weights off it, $\vartheta_t$ collects the
effects of interest and $B_t$ the approximation errors. Solving it,
$\hat\vartheta_t^{\text{iSCM}} = \hat\Omega^{-1}\hat\beta_t$, removes the
contamination without modifying the underlying estimator.

## Commands at a glance

| I want to... | Command |
|---|---|
| estimate the full iSCM | `iscm(data, id, time, outcome, treated, affected, t0)` |
| estimate the simplified iSCM | `iscm(..., simplified = TRUE)` |
| estimate the restricted SCM | `restricted_scm(...)` (same arguments) |
| get the unrestricted (uncorrected) SCM | `fit$gaps_unrestricted` |
| see effects and diagnostics | `fit`, `summary(fit)`, `fit$effects`, `fit$diagnostics` |
| plot the gaps | `plot(fit, unit = ..., restricted = ...)` |
| plot observed vs synthetic outcomes, or the weights | `plot(fit, type = "trends")`, `plot(fit, type = "weights")` |
| choose among the specifications | `iscm_compare(...)` |
| run the placebo analysis | `iscm_placebo(fit, data, id, time, outcome, target = ...)` |
| vary the set of affected units | `iscm_sensitivity(..., affected_sets = list(...))` |
| use another SC-type estimator | `iscm(..., estimator = scm_penalized)`, `scm_synth`, or your own function |
| correct fits estimated elsewhere | `iscm_assemble(gaps, weights, t0)` |

iSCM sorts the units into three groups: the **main treated unit**; the
**potentially affected units** (the set $M$), which may also have been affected
by the intervention, because treated as well or exposed to spillovers, and which
stay in the donor pool; and the **pure controls**, all remaining units, assumed
unaffected.

All data-level functions take the same first arguments:

| Argument | What it is |
|---|---|
| `data` | a balanced panel in long format (one row per unit and period) |
| `id`, `time`, `outcome` | names of the columns with the unit identifier, the period and the outcome |
| `treated` | identifier of the main treated unit |
| `affected` | identifiers of the potentially affected units; every other unit is a pure control |
| `t0` | last pre-intervention period |
| `predictors` | optional: columns used for matching, averaged over the pre-intervention period; if omitted, units are matched on the pre-intervention outcome path |

## 1. Estimate

`simulate_iscm()` draws a factor-model panel with a main treated unit `TR`, one
potentially affected unit `A1` and six pure controls `C1`–`C6`. Here the true
effect on `TR` is `2` and the spillover on `A1` is `3`.

```{r sim}
sim <- simulate_iscm(n_affected = 1, n_pure = 6, tau = 2, spill = 3, seed = 7)
head(sim$data)

fit <- iscm(sim$data, id = "unit", time = "time", outcome = "Y",
            treated = "TR", affected = "A1", t0 = sim$t0)
fit
```

`print()` reports the average post-intervention effects and the conditioning of
$\hat\Omega$. `summary()` gives the effects period by period, and the estimates
are stored as a matrix in `fit$effects` (row 1: main treated unit; other rows:
affected units).

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

The inclusive and unrestricted gaps coincide before the intervention, because the
correction only applies afterwards. With simulated data, `truth` adds the true
effect as a reference line: zero before the intervention, `sim$tau` after it.

```{r plot}
rest <- restricted_scm(sim$data, "unit", "time", "Y",
                       treated = "TR", affected = "A1", t0 = sim$t0)
plot(fit, restricted = rest, truth = sim$tau)
```

### The four specifications side by side

Section 5.1 of the paper recommends always reporting four specifications: the
unrestricted SCM (affected units kept, no correction), the restricted SCM
(affected units dropped), and the full and simplified iSCM.

```{r four}
fit_s <- iscm(sim$data, "unit", "time", "Y", "TR", "A1", sim$t0,
              simplified = TRUE)
post <- fit$times > sim$t0
c(truth        = 2,
  unrestricted = mean(fit$gaps_unrestricted[post, "TR"]),
  restricted   = mean(rest$gap[post]),
  full_iSCM    = mean(fit$effects["TR", ]),
  simpl_iSCM   = mean(fit_s$effects["TR", ]))
```

The unrestricted estimate is contaminated: it equals
$\theta_t - \hat w_2\gamma_t$ up to approximation error, so the positive
spillover on `A1`, which receives weight `r round(fit$fits$TR$w[["A1"]], 2)`,
pulls it well below the true value. Both versions of iSCM remove the
contamination. iSCM also recovers the spillover itself:

```{r gamma}
mean(fit$effects["A1", ])   # true spillover = 3
```

In this simulated design the restricted SCM performs well too, because the pure
controls alone reproduce `TR` well. This is not an accident: Lemma 3.1 shows that
the iSCM counterfactual is itself a weighted average of pure controls, so when the
restricted SCM matches directly on the pre-intervention outcome path it can find
an equally good combination. Section 3.1 explains when iSCM gains: when the
restricted optimizer, guided by its own criterion, picks a worse combination of
pure controls than the one implied by iSCM.

### When the affected unit is essential

`simulate_iscm_covariates()` builds such a case. Units are matched on two
observed covariates, `x1` and `x2`; the outcome also depends on an unobserved
characteristic $u$. `TR` and `A1` are close to each other and share $u = 1$ (think
of West Germany and Austria). Two pure controls close to `TR` in covariates,
`C3` and `C4`, have $u = 0$; the pure controls with $u = 1$, `C1` and `C2`, lie on
either side of the pair, farther from `TR` than `A1`. Without `A1`, the
restricted optimizer can match the covariates equally well with `C1` and `C2`
(right $u$) or with `C1`, `C3` and `C4` (wrong $u$), and which one it picks
depends on the noise. We
use the penalized SCM of Abadie and L'Hour (2021), `scm_penalized`, which
favours donors close to the focal unit.

```{r cov-design}
sim_c <- simulate_iscm_covariates(seed = 4)   # true effects: 2 on TR, 3 on A1
args <- list(sim_c$data, "unit", "time", "Y", "TR", "A1", sim_c$t0,
             predictors = c("x1", "x2"), estimator = scm_penalized)

fit_c   <- do.call(iscm, args)
fit_cs  <- do.call(iscm, c(args, simplified = TRUE))
rest_c  <- do.call(restricted_scm, args)
post_c  <- fit_c$times > sim_c$t0
c(truth        = 2,
  unrestricted = mean(fit_c$gaps_unrestricted[post_c, "TR"]),
  restricted   = mean(rest_c$gap[post_c]),
  full_iSCM    = mean(fit_c$effects["TR", ]),
  simpl_iSCM   = mean(fit_cs$effects["TR", ]))
```

The weights show why. With `A1` available, `TR` is reproduced by `A1` and `C1`,
both with the right unobserved characteristic; without it, in this replication
the restricted SCM leans on `C3` and `C4`, which match the covariates but not
$u$. The implied weights of iSCM recover a combination of pure controls with the
right $u$:

```{r cov-weights}
round(rbind(unrestricted = fit_c$fits$TR$w[c("A1", sim_c$pure)],
            restricted   = c(A1 = NA, rest_c$w[sim_c$pure]),
            iSCM_implied = c(A1 = NA, fit_c$implied_weights[sim_c$pure])), 2)
```

The simplified iSCM is accurate too, because the restricted fit of `A1` can rely
on `C2`, which has the right $u$. iSCM also recovers the spillover:

```{r cov-gamma}
mean(fit_c$effects["A1", ])   # true spillover = 3
```

The plot of the gaps, with the true effect as a reference, shows the three
estimators at work:

```{r cov-plot}
plot(fit_c, restricted = rest_c, truth = sim_c$tau)
```

- **Before the intervention**, a good synthetic control has a gap close to zero.
  This holds for the unrestricted fit, and hence for iSCM, which coincides with
  it before the intervention. The restricted gap drifts away from zero instead:
  its donors `C3` and `C4` match the covariates but not $u$, whose effect on the
  outcome grows over time. This poor pre-intervention fit is the warning sign
  that the decision rule of Section 5.1 picks up.
- **After the intervention**, iSCM follows the true effect. The unrestricted SCM
  is pulled below it, by the weight of `A1` times its positive spillover: this is
  the contamination that iSCM removes. The restricted SCM overshoots, because the
  bias already visible before the intervention carries over. Its jump at the
  intervention happens to be close to the true effect here, but reading the
  effect that way would assume that the bias stays constant, which nothing
  guarantees: the estimate of the restricted SCM is its gap, and the gap is far
  from the truth.

The same plot for the affected unit shows that iSCM also recovers the spillover
on `A1`, which the unrestricted SCM underestimates:

```{r cov-plot-a1}
plot(fit_c, unit = c("TR", "A1"),
     truth = list(TR = sim_c$tau, A1 = sim_c$spill))
```

Plots are drawn with `ggplot2`, so they can be modified with the usual
`ggplot2` functions. `type = "trends"` compares the observed outcome with the
synthetic ones, and `type = "weights"` shows the donor weights next to the
implied weights on the pure controls:

```{r cov-plot-more}
plot(fit_c, type = "trends", restricted = rest_c)
plot(fit_c, type = "weights")
```

## 2. Check the diagnostics

The reliability of the correction depends on the conditioning of $\hat\Omega$.
Every fit stores the diagnostics of `omega_diagnostics()`:

```{r diag}
fit$Omega
fit$diagnostics[c("det", "sigma_min", "amplification", "alpha", "diag_dominant")]
```

`amplification` $= 1/\sigma_{\min}(\hat\Omega)$ bounds how much the correction can
magnify the approximation errors of the underlying fits (Theorem 2.1(a)); for a
single affected unit, $\alpha = 1/(1-\hat w_2\hat l_1)$ is the corresponding
factor in closed form. Values close to one, as here, mean the correction is
stable. When the cross-weights are large, the **simplified iSCM**
(`simplified = TRUE`) avoids the inversion altogether.

The implied weights show the iSCM counterfactual as a weighted average of pure
controls only (Lemma 3.1):

```{r implied}
round(fit$implied_weights, 3)
```

## 3. Choose the specification

`iscm_compare()` runs the decision rule of Section 5.1:

1. **Step 1.** If the potentially affected units receive negligible weight in the
   unrestricted fit, all specifications should agree: restricted SCM.
2. **Steps 2 and 3.** Compare the predictor imbalance and the pre-intervention
   RMSPE of the unrestricted and restricted fits. By default the RMSPE is
   computed on a validation window: the weights are estimated on the first two
   thirds of the pre-intervention period and evaluated on the last third. A ratio
   below 1.25 means the fits are comparable; from 1.5 on, the restricted fit is
   substantially worse. If neither the imbalance nor the RMSPE is substantially
   worse, the rule keeps the restricted SCM, which avoids amplifying the
   approximation errors.
3. **Step 4.** Otherwise the iSCM correction is warranted. If the amplification
   factor $\alpha$ (or $1/\sigma_{\min}$ with several affected units) is below
   1.25, the full iSCM is applied. If not, the simplified iSCM is chosen when the
   restricted fits of the affected units remain adequate; when they are poor
   too, no variant can be considered reliable, and the set $M$ should be
   reconsidered (Section 5.2).

Steps 2 and 3 are also reported for each affected unit.

```{r compare-specs}
cmp <- iscm_compare(sim$data, "unit", "time", "Y", "TR", "A1", sim$t0)
cmp
```

In the covariate design the restricted fit is much worse and $\alpha$ is below
1.25, so the rule recommends the full iSCM:

```{r compare-cov}
cmp_c <- do.call(iscm_compare, args)
cmp_c$recommendation
cmp_c$alpha
```

The thresholds (`weight_tol`, `comparable_tol`, `worse_tol`, `alpha_tol`), the
validation window and the standardisation of the imbalance can be changed; see
`?iscm_compare`. The rule selects the specification to emphasise; all four should
still be reported. The printed output also shows the pre-intervention RMSPE of
the counterfactuals implied by the full and the simplified iSCM, an additional
diagnostic of the trade-off in equations (4.6) and (4.7); `rule = "implied_rmspe"`
uses it in Step 4 instead of the threshold on $\alpha$.

If the synthetic controls were estimated outside the package, use
`iscm_compare_fits()` with their gaps and weights, or `iscm_decision()` with the
summary figures. With the German-reunification figures of Section 7 (validation
RMSPE 358.09 for the restricted fit against 93.08, standardised imbalance 1.50
against 0.26, $\alpha \approx 1.16$):

```{r decision}
iscm_decision(rmspe_ratio = 358.09 / 93.08, imbalance_ratio = 1.50 / 0.26,
              alpha = 1.16)
```

## 4. Placebo inference

`iscm_placebo()` implements the in-space placebo analysis of
[Section 6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.17624).
Outcomes of the affected units are purged of their estimated effects, the
intervention is reassigned to each pure control in turn, and the post- to
pre-intervention RMSPE ratios are compared. Run it for the main treated unit and
for each affected unit.

```{r placebo}
pb <- iscm_placebo(fit, sim$data, "unit", "time", "Y", target = "TR")
pb
plot(pb)
plot(pb, type = "gaps")

iscm_placebo(fit, sim$data, "unit", "time", "Y", target = "A1")
```

The printed result also reports what Section 6 recommends stating
alongside the p-value: the smallest attainable p-value, here $1/7$ with six pure
controls, and the conditioning of $\hat\Omega$, since the statistic of the
target is tilted upwards when $\alpha$ is far from one.

When the synthetic controls were estimated outside the package, the placebo
works in three steps: `iscm_purge()` returns the data with the estimated effects
removed from the focal units; you estimate the synthetic control of each pure
control on those data with your own estimator; `iscm_placebo_fits()` computes
the statistics from the weights. The German replication script below uses this
route with the paper's `Synth` specification.

## 5. Sensitivity to the set of affected units

The choice of affected units should be motivated economically and focus on units
that receive non-negligible weight (Section 5.2). `iscm_sensitivity()`
re-estimates iSCM under alternative sets and reports the effect and the
conditioning side by side, together with the weights each candidate receives in
the unrestricted fit.

```{r sensitivity}
sim2 <- simulate_iscm(n_affected = 2, n_pure = 6, tau = 2, spill = c(3, 1), seed = 5)
iscm_sensitivity(sim2$data, "unit", "time", "Y", treated = "TR",
                 affected_sets = list(minimal = "A1", extended = c("A1", "A2")),
                 t0 = sim2$t0)
```

## 6. Using a different SC-type estimator

iSCM works on top of any estimator whose counterfactual is a weighted average of
donor outcomes. There are three ways to plug one in.

**A built-in backend.** `scm_base` (the default) solves the classic
simplex-constrained problem with fixed predictor weights and needs no other
package. `scm_penalized` adds the penalty of Abadie and L'Hour (2021), passed
as `lambda`. `scm_synth` calls `Synth::synth`, which also optimises the predictor
weights:

```{r synth-backend, eval = FALSE}
iscm(sim$data, "unit", "time", "Y", "TR", "A1", sim$t0, estimator = scm_synth)
```

**Your own backend.** Any function with signature
`function(X1, X0, v = NULL, ...)` that returns donor weights can be used; see
`?backends`.

**Your own fits.** When the specification cannot be expressed through `iscm()`,
for example `Synth::dataprep` with special predictors and different time windows,
or a penalized estimator, estimate the synthetic controls yourself and pass the
gap series and donor weights of each focal unit to `iscm_assemble()`. The
next section does this for the paper's application.

## 7. Replicating the German-reunification application

The paper estimates the effect of reunification on West Germany's GDP per capita,
allowing for spillovers on Austria, with the `Synth` specification of Abadie et
al. (2015). The `germany` panel ships with the package. The two unrestricted
synthetic controls are estimated with `Synth` and handed to `iscm_assemble()`.

```{r germany, eval = requireNamespace("Synth", quietly = TRUE), results = "hide", message = FALSE}
library(Synth)
data(germany)
x <- germany
key <- unique(x[, c("index", "country")])
named <- function(w) setNames(as.numeric(w),
  key$country[match(as.integer(rownames(w)), key$index)])

# --- West Germany (unit 7): V cross-validated on 1971-80, weights on 1960-89 ---
dp_tr <- dataprep(x, predictors = c("gdp","trade","infrate"), dependent = "gdp",
  unit.variable = 1, time.variable = 3,
  special.predictors = list(list("industry",1971:1980,"mean"),
    list("schooling",c(1970,1975),"mean"), list("invest70",1980,"mean")),
  treatment.identifier = 7, controls.identifier = unique(x$index)[-7],
  time.predictors.prior = 1971:1980, time.optimize.ssr = 1981:1990,
  unit.names.variable = 2, time.plot = 1960:2003)
so_tr <- synth(dp_tr, Margin.ipop = .005, Sigf.ipop = 7, Bound.ipop = 6)
dp_wg <- dataprep(x, predictors = c("gdp","trade","infrate"), dependent = "gdp",
  unit.variable = 1, time.variable = 3,
  special.predictors = list(list("industry",1981:1990,"mean"),
    list("schooling",c(1980,1985),"mean"), list("invest80",1980,"mean")),
  treatment.identifier = 7, controls.identifier = unique(x$index)[-7],
  time.predictors.prior = 1981:1990, time.optimize.ssr = 1960:1989,
  unit.names.variable = 2, time.plot = 1960:2003)
so_wg <- synth(dp_wg, custom.v = as.numeric(so_tr$solution.v))
gap_wg <- as.numeric(dp_wg$Y1plot - dp_wg$Y0plot %*% so_wg$solution.w)

# --- Austria (unit 3): data-driven V ---
dp_au <- dataprep(x, predictors = c("gdp","trade","infrate"), dependent = "gdp",
  unit.variable = 1, time.variable = 3,
  special.predictors = list(list("industry",1971:1990,"mean"),
    list("schooling",c(1970,1985),"mean"), list("invest80",1980,"mean")),
  treatment.identifier = 3, controls.identifier = unique(x$index)[-3],
  time.predictors.prior = 1971:1990, time.optimize.ssr = 1960:1989,
  unit.names.variable = 2, time.plot = 1960:2003)
so_au <- synth(dp_au, Margin.ipop = .005, Sigf.ipop = 7, Bound.ipop = 6)
gap_au <- as.numeric(dp_au$Y1plot - dp_au$Y0plot %*% so_au$solution.w)
```

```{r germany-iscm, eval = requireNamespace("Synth", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_ger <- iscm_assemble(
  gaps    = list("West Germany" = gap_wg, "Austria" = gap_au),
  weights = list("West Germany" = named(so_wg$solution.w),
                 "Austria"      = named(so_au$solution.w)),
  t0 = 1989, times = 1960:2003,
  pure = setdiff(key$country, c("West Germany", "Austria")))
fit_ger
```

This reproduces the paper: West Germany's synthetic control gives Austria a
weight of about `0.42` and Austria's gives West Germany about `0.33`, so
$\hat\Omega$ has determinant `0.86`, smallest singular value `0.62` and
$\alpha \approx 1.16$. The average effect on West Germany is about `-1,677`
dollars per year, against `-1,570` for the unrestricted SCM, and the spillover on
Austria is about `-254`.

The complete replication, with the restricted and simplified specifications, the
decision rule, Tables 1–3, Figure 1 and the placebo analysis (with
`iscm_purge()` and `iscm_placebo_fits()`), is in a script installed with the
package; a second script reproduces the inclusive
penalized SCM of Section 7.1:

```{r scripts, eval = FALSE}
system.file("examples", "germany_replication.R", package = "iscm")
system.file("examples", "germany_penalized.R",   package = "iscm")
```
